title: Right-Triangle Trig & the Unit Circle
summary: Trig ratios sine, cosine, and tangent relate a right triangle's angles to its sides (SOH-CAH-TOA). The unit circle extends these to all angles, with coordinates $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and special angles $30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ$ giving exact values.

sine.plain: Opposite over hypotenuse in a right triangle.

SOH-CAH-TOA.plain: Memory aid for the three ratios.

unit circle.plain: A circle of radius 1 centered at the origin.

radian.plain: An angle measure based on arc length.

reference angle.in_class: Gives the magnitude of trig values in any quadrant.

concept_sections.heading: The three ratios
concept_sections.explanation: In a right triangle, sine, cosine, and tangent are fixed ratios of the sides for a given acute angle — SOH-CAH-TOA. They let you find unknown sides or angles.
math_steps: Label opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse relative to the angle.
Pick the ratio with your known and unknown sides.

concept_sections.heading: Solving right triangles
concept_sections.explanation: Given an angle and a side, use a trig ratio to find another side; given two sides, use an inverse trig function to find the angle.
math_steps: Choose the ratio linking known and unknown.
Set up and solve the equation.

concept_sections.heading: Special right triangles
concept_sections.explanation: The 45-45-90 triangle has sides $1:1:\sqrt2$; the 30-60-90 has $1:\sqrt3:2$. These give exact trig values for $30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ$.

concept_sections.heading: The unit circle
concept_sections.explanation: On the unit circle, the point at angle $\theta$ has coordinates $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. This defines sine and cosine for every angle, positive or negative.
math_steps: Place the angle from the positive $x$-axis.

concept_sections.heading: Radians and reference angles
concept_sections.explanation: Convert degrees and radians with $180^\circ=\pi$. In any quadrant, the reference angle gives the value's size; the quadrant gives the sign.
math_steps: Find the reference angle to the $x$-axis.
